Tidal locking, a phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, profoundly shapes planetary climates across the universe. As one hemisphere perpetually faces its star while the other remains in eternal darkness, this configuration creates some of the most extreme climate conditions known to science.

The most dramatic consequence is the stark temperature divide between hemispheres. On tidally locked worlds like those around red dwarf stars—the most common stars in our galaxy—dayside temperatures can soar above 2,000°C on close-orbiting planets, while nightside temperatures plummet to hundreds of degrees below zero. This thermal contrast drives powerful atmospheric dynamics: air heated on the dayside rises, flows across the terminator (the boundary between day and night), and sinks on the nightside, creating persistent winds that can exceed the speed of sound on some worlds.

Atmospheres themselves face existential threats. Scientists once theorized that tidally locked planets might have their atmospheres completely frozen out on the nightside, a scenario called atmospheric collapse. While modeling suggests vigorous day-night heat transport can prevent this catastrophe, the risk remains real for thin atmospheres. Tidal locking, a phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, profoundly shapes planetary climates in ways that challenge our Earth-centric assumptions about habitability.

The most dramatic examples orbit red dwarf stars, the most common stars in our galaxy. Planets close enough to these dim stars to maintain liquid water become tidally locked, with one hemisphere in perpetual daylight and the other in eternal night. This creates one of the most extreme temperature contrasts imaginable: the dayside of a locked planet can reach 2,000°C while the nightside plunges to -200°C, a difference exceeding anything in our solar system.

Yet tidal locking doesn't necessarily preclude habitability. Climate models suggest that if a locked planet retains a substantial atmosphere, winds redistribute heat from dayside to nightside, moderating both extremes. The terminator zone—the permanent twilight band between hemispheres—could host a temperate "eyeball" climate where liquid water persists. Some models even predict a permanent dayside ocean surrounded by nightside ice, resembling a staring eye when viewed from space.

Atmospheric collapse poses the greatest threat. Without sufficient atmosphere, air on the nightside condenses and freezes onto the surface, a process called atmospheric collapse or "air trapping." This would strip the planet of its protective blanket, exposing the surface to vacuum conditions.
